extracted.intended_audience: law students, video game developers, legal practitioners, and general readers interested in video game copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative considerations used to determine whether one video game unlawfully copies another, focusing on protectability of elements, substantial similarity, and applicable doctrines and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merger doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal principle where courts will not grant copyright protection where it would effectively give someone a monopoly over an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by Judge William H. Orrick Jr. in this case; used to refuse protection when idea and expression merge. Example language from the court: 'copyright protection does not encompass games as such, since they consist of abstract rules and play ideas.' The doctrine prevents extending protection if it would monopolize underlying ideas or gameplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scènes à faire / standard elements are unprotectable
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic concepts, functional rules, and scènes à faire are not protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court treated many similarities (e.g., commonplace kicks and punches, stereotyped characters) as scènes à faire. The page notes that 'the vast majority of the moves are unprotectable because they are commonplace kicks and punches.' This criterion is used to exclude ordinary or stock elements of a genre from protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea-expression dichotomy: games/rules not copyrightable
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright does not protect game ideas or abstract rules and play ideas; protection covers expression, not ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum emphasizes that 'audiovisual works like the two presently before the Court are largely unprotectable games.' This supports evaluating whether the challenged material is an idea/rule (unprotectable) or a particular expressive form (potentially protectable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity of protectable elements required for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all copying is infringing; the copied elements must be protectable expression and there must be substantial similarity between protectable elements of the works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts K.C. Munchkin!/Pac‑Man (court found substantial similarities and infringement) with other cases where similarity in non-protectable elements did not suffice. Courts analyze whether the similarities identified are of the kind that copyright protects and whether they are substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive characters and specific audiovisual elements can be protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characters and specific expressive elements (e.g., unique character designs or uniquely-expressed special moves) may qualify as protectable expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court identified that 'of the eight pairs of characters and twenty-seven special moves at issue, three characters and five special moves in Fighter’s History are similar to protectable characters and special moves in Street Fighter II.' This shows courts parse which characters/moves are protectable and which are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative and contextual weighing of similarities (proportion of copied material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider the amount and proportion of similar material in the context of the whole work when assessing infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court noted Street Fighter II had 'a total universe of twelve characters and six hundred and fifty moves' and that the 'vast majority' of moves were commonplace; this comparison of how much of the work is allegedly copied (and whether the copied share is protectable) informs the ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and evolving case law shape protectability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior rulings (e.g., Atari v. Philips, Data East v. Epyx, Tetris v. Xio, Spry Fox v. Lolapps) are used to determine what game elements are protectable; the legal approach has shifted over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces a trend: earlier rulings often found clones permissibly unprotectable, but later cases (2012 onward) enforced narrower limits and protected more specific copying. Parties invoke precedents to argue for or against protection of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of intent or copying does not automatically establish infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where design documents or other evidence show intentional imitation, infringement depends on whether the copied material is protected expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data East's design documents referred to Street Fighter II and some evidence showed imitation, but the court ruled elements copied were unprotectable, so intent alone did not produce liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of expert testimony on commonplace/genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert witnesses may testify that particular features are conventional in the genre and thus not protectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Kunkel testified (citing Atari v. Philips) that not all copying is infringing because some similarities reflect standard genre conventions; such testimony helps courts classify elements as scènes à faire or common.
